title: I Tried a High-Tech Package Locker Before the Holiday Shopping Rush
gist: WIRED rates the $297 Hyve Smart Package Locker 7/10. It is a PIN-based, Wi-Fi-bridged lockbox of 7.4 cubic feet that Hyve says fits 80% of Amazon package sizes, with paid tiers of $5/month for per-carrier PINs and $15/month for return pickups available only in LA and Seattle. The main obstacle was getting couriers to use it: drivers first ignored it, then FedEx, UPS and Amazon reached about 75% use, at which point the box filled up within a day or two.

insights.claim: According to the reviewer, FedEx quietly discontinued its vacation hold option in 2026 without a formal announcement, which a FedEx rep later confirmed. Holding packages at shipping centers or access points typically costs about $5 per package.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: Carriers are cutting hold services, which leaves room for third-party secure-delivery hardware and subscription products.
insights.locator: Package hold requests aren’t consistently honored

insights.claim: FedEx and UPS have replaced free-form delivery instruction fields with simplified drop-down menus that offer no 'lockbox' option. That makes it structurally hard for homeowners to direct drivers to a smart locker.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: Smart-locker adoption depends on carrier software integration; without it, products like Hyve struggle to get used.
insights.locator: Both FedEx and UPS, for example

insights.claim: The Hyve locker costs $297. It is 32x20x20 inches with 7.4 cubic feet of capacity, which Hyve says fits 80% of Amazon package sizes. It opens with 4-digit PINs, needs an indoor Wi-Fi bridge, runs on four AA batteries with solar trickle charging, and requires about an hour of flat-pack assembly with no printed instructions.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: High setup friction and a $297 price limit the product to a niche, mass-market appeal is doubtful.
insights.locator: The Hyve Smart Package Locker is a play

insights.claim: Hyve says AA batteries should last five to six months, but the reviewer's first set died within three weeks without warning, and he needed USB-C emergency power.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: Reliability problems in early hardware are a risk for consumer-IoT startups.
insights.locator: The unit is powered by four AA batteries

insights.claim: Hyve earns recurring revenue on top of the hardware: Essentials ($5/month or $50/year) adds per-carrier PINs and access logs, and the Returns Plan ($15/month) adds twice-monthly return pickups by Hyve's own couriers, but only in Los Angeles and Seattle.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: A hardware-plus-subscription model whose most valuable tier is limited by courier logistics; the reviewer expects any rollout to other regions to be slow.
insights.locator: If you want more fine-grained security

insights.claim: Without the Returns Plan, Essentials users can schedule returns through Uber Courier, which cost the reviewer $8-18 per Amazon return. That makes the $15/month plan with two pickups much better value where it is offered.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: Shows what consumers pay for on-demand last-mile return pickups.
insights.locator: If you don’t have the Hyve Returns subscription

themes.theme: Driver adoption is the core problem

insights.claim: In the first days, couriers left packages next to the locker. One FedEx driver had turned down the volume on his device, which gives spoken delivery instructions. After an in-person demo he used the box, but his replacement on the route ignored it again.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: Whether a smart locker works depends on individual driver behavior that the homeowner cannot control or enforce.
insights.locator: The next day, I encountered the FedEx driver

insights.claim: After the initial weeks, FedEx, UPS and Amazon drivers began using the locker regularly; the reviewer estimated about 75% of deliveries went into it. At that rate, one multi-box UPS drop could fill it, so it could not hold more than a day or two of deliveries.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: The product partly fails at its main use case (going away for a week) for heavy-delivery households.
insights.locator: I was about to give up

insights.claim: Hyve's CEO acknowledged that drivers not using the box is a problem for many homeowners. The company supplies an adhesive sign and promotes a 'Snack Stop' placard with free snacks inside to get drivers to open the box.
insights.speaker: Christopher Null
insights.so_what: A company workaround of snacks for drivers shows that the delivery ecosystem has no built-in way to make couriers use the box.
insights.locator: Early on in my testing, I spoke to Hyve
